hypotheses.title: Redeem request replay via missing nonce deduplication
hypotheses.description: `requestRedeem` verifies the order signature but never calls `_deduplicateOrder(order.userWallet, order.nonce)`, unlike `mint` and `depositIncome`. The only replay guard is the `requestId` uniqueness check, but the requestId is attacker-controlled via `order.additionalData` and can be varied arbitrarily while keeping the same signed order fields. The same signed order can therefore be submitted repeatedly with different requestIds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Obtain one valid signed REDEEM order from the trusted signer. 2) Call `requestRedeem` with requestId "A" — YUSD is locked and a request is created. 3) Call `requestRedeem` again with the same order but requestId "B" — signature still valid, nonce never consumed. 4) Repeat with requestIds "C", "D", ... Each call locks `order.yusdAmount` from the user and creates a new pending redeem request.
hypotheses.impact: A single signed order can be replayed to create unlimited redeem requests, each locking YUSD and each eligible for collateral payout on approval. This drains collateral reserves and inflates `totalRedeemLockedYUSD`, causing insolvency and double-spend of the same signed authorization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_deduplicateOrder(order.userWallet, order.nonce)` inside `requestRedeem` immediately after `order.verify(...)`, matching the pattern used in `mint` and `depositIncome`.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRedeemRequest lacks caller/benefactor check, anyone can trigger
hypotheses.description: withdrawRedeemRequest() has no access modifier and does not verify that _msgSender() is the order's userWallet or any authorized party. Any external caller can invoke it for any expired PENDING redeem request, forcing the locked YUSD to be returned to the user and marking the request WITHDRAWN. While funds go to the legitimate user, this lets an attacker grief the protocol by prematurely closing requests that FUNDS_MANAGER intended to approve, and it can be used to front-run approveRedeemRequest.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a PENDING redeem request whose order.expiry has passed. 2) Attacker calls withdrawRedeemRequest(requestId) directly. 3) Request is marked WITHDRAWN and YUSD is returned to user, blocking any subsequent approveRedeemRequest (which requires status PENDING).
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on redeem approvals; griefing of protocol operations; potential accounting churn on totalRedeemLockedYUSD.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict withdrawRedeemRequest to the order.userWallet (or an authorized role) via a check like `if (_msgSender() != request.order.userWallet) revert NotWhitelisted();` or add an appropriate modifier.

hypotheses.title: Missing staleness check on AegisOracle YUSD/USD price
hypotheses.description: `AegisOracle.yusdUSDPrice()` returns `_priceData.price` with no check that the price is fresh. The contract tracks `lastUpdateTimestamp` but never enforces a maximum age. `AegisMinting._getAssetYUSDPriceOracle()` consumes this price to compute redeem collateral amounts and never verifies freshness either. A stale (but nonzero) price will be silently used, skewing collateral calculations in favor of one party.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator-signed price becomes stale after some time. The AegisOracle is never updated (operator offline, missed tx). A whitelisted user calls `requestRedeem` or `approveRedeemRequest`; `_calculateRedeemMinCollateralAmount` uses the stale YUSD price to determine the min collateral amount, letting the user redeem at an outdated rate that no longer reflects reality.
hypotheses.impact: Users can redeem YUSD for collateral at a stale price, draining more (or less) collateral than the fair market rate, causing insolvency or asset imbalance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a max-age (heartbeat) check on `_priceData.timestamp` inside `yusdUSDPrice()` or in `_getAssetYUSDPriceOracle` and revert/return zero if stale.

hypotheses.title: Redeem request can be permanently blocked by front-running requestId
hypotheses.description: The requestId is supplied by the user inside `order.additionalData` and is not bound to the user or nonce. Any whitelisted attacker can observe a victim's pending redeem transaction in the mempool, extract the requestId, and submit their own `requestRedeem` with the same requestId first. The check `if (request.timestamp != 0) revert InvalidRedeemRequest();` then permanently blocks the victim from ever using that requestId, and the victim's signed order (with its nonce) is now unusable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted) sees victim's `requestRedeem` tx in mempool. 2) Attacker copies `order.additionalData` (the requestId string) and submits their own valid signed redeem order with the same requestId, higher gas. 3) Attacker's tx lands first, storing `_redeemRequests[keccak256(requestId)]` with `timestamp != 0`. 4) Victim's tx reverts with `InvalidRedeemRequest`. 5) Attacker can repeat for every victim requestId, or simply leave the request PENDING forever (never approved/rejected/withdrawn) to lock the slot.
hypotheses.impact: Victims cannot create redeem requests with their intended requestId; if the attacker never resolves the request, the requestId slot is permanently occupied. Combined with off-chain signing flows that pre-commit to a requestId, this can freeze the entire redeem path for targeted users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the requestId to `order.userWallet` (e.g., include msg.sender in the hash) or require the requestId to be derived from the order nonce/signature so it cannot be pre-empted by another account.

hypotheses.title: Missing deadline check on mint/requestRedeem/depositIncome orders
hypotheses.description: `OrderLib.Order` contains an `expiry` field, but `mint` and `depositIncome` never check `order.expiry >= block.timestamp`. Only `requestRedeem`'s downstream `approveRedeemRequest`/`withdrawRedeemRequest` paths reference expiry. A signed mint order therefore remains valid indefinitely, and a signed depositIncome order likewise. If the trusted signer rotates or the price moves, an old signed order can still be executed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Trusted signer signs a MINT order at a favorable price. 2) The order is not executed immediately. 3) Later, after prices move against the protocol, an attacker (the order's userWallet, who is whitelisted) submits the stale signed order. 4) `mint` accepts it because expiry is never checked, minting YUSD at the old favorable rate.
hypotheses.impact: Stale signed orders can be executed at outdated prices, causing the protocol to mint YUSD against collateral at unfavorable rates and incurring losses to the protocol/insurance fund.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (order.expiry < block.timestamp) revert OrderExpired();` in `mint` and `depositIncome` (and confirm `requestRedeem` enforces it at creation time).

hypotheses.title: Reward claim allows partial amounts leaving reward claimable again
hypotheses.description: `claimRewards` marks `_addressClaimedRewards[msg.sender][id] = true` on the first claim, but it subtracts only `claimRequest.amounts[i]` from `_rewards[id].amount`. If the user supplies an amount smaller than the reward, the remaining balance stays in `_rewards[id].amount`, yet the user is permanently flagged as having claimed that id, so the residual is stranded. Conversely, if the same id appears twice in `claimRequest.ids`, the second iteration is skipped by the `_addressClaimedRewards` check, so no double-claim there — but the residual stranding is the flaw.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted user with a valid signed claim request) submits a claim for id `A` with `amounts[0] = 1` wei while `_rewards[A].amount = 1000e18`. 2) `_addressClaimedRewards[attacker][A] = true`, `_rewards[A].amount -= 1`. 3) Attacker can never claim the remaining 999.999...e18 because the flag blocks re-claim, and `withdrawExpiredRewards` only sends to a manager-chosen `to`. 4) The residual is effectively burned from the user's perspective but still counted in the contract's YUSD balance.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose the bulk of their rewards; the contract holds YUSD that is neither claimable nor withdrawable by the user, breaking reward accounting and locking funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `claimRequest.amounts[i] == _rewards[id].amount` (full claim) or only set the claimed flag when the reward balance reaches zero.

hypotheses.title: Redeem fee charged on full yusdAmount while collateral computed from same amount
hypotheses.description: In approveRedeemRequest, collateralAmount is computed from request.order.yusdAmount (the full locked amount) via _calculateRedeemMinCollateralAmount, but the fee is then deducted from yusdAmount to produce burnAmount. The user receives collateral for the full yusdAmount while only burnAmount YUSD is burned and fee is transferred to insuranceFund. The collateral paid out corresponds to the pre-fee amount, so the protocol pays out more collateral than the net YUSD burned, causing a value leak from the collateral pool to the redeemer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted) submits requestRedeem with yusdAmount Y and collateralAmount C. 2) FUNDS_MANAGER approves with amount = C. 3) collateralAmount computed from Y (full), fee = Y*redeemFeeBP/10000 transferred to insuranceFund, burnAmount = Y - fee burned. 4) Attacker receives collateral worth Y but only Y-fee YUSD is burned; the fee is effectively paid by the collateral pool, not the redeemer.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral pool drained by fee amount per redeem; accounting drift between YUSD burned and collateral released; protocol insolvency over time.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute collateralAmount from burnAmount (net of fee) rather than request.order.yusdAmount, or deduct the fee from the collateral payout.

hypotheses.title: assetChainlinkUSDPrice / assetAegisOracleYUSDPrice revert or return 0 without heartbeat validation for unconfigured assets
hypotheses.description: The staleness check uses `chainlinkAssetHeartbeat[asset]` which is only set in `_addSupportedAsset` and `setChainlinkAssetHeartbeat`. If `removeSupportedAsset` is called, the heartbeat is zeroed but the asset may still be referenced in an existing pending RedeemRequest; `approveRedeemRequest` re-validates support and would reject, but `_calculateMinYUSDAmount` during `mint` similarly uses the Chainlink price. Also, `assetChainlinkUSDPrice()` (public view) reverts when the feed is stale — callers relying on it must handle reverts, not staleness. In `_calculateMinYUSDAmount`, if `chainlinkPrice == 0`, the function silently returns `yusdAmount` (the user-supplied value), removing oracle protection entirely.
hypotheses.attackPath: Admin disables `_feedRegistry` (set to address(0)) via `setFeedRegistryAddress` — this is allowed — after which `_getAssetUSDPriceChainlink` returns `(0,0)`. Then `_calculateMinYUSDAmount` returns `yusdAmount` directly, and `_calculateRedeemMinCollateralAmount` skips the Chainlink adjustment and only uses AegisOracle (which also may be zero). A user-supplied `yusdAmount`/`collateralAmount` becomes the sole arbiter, letting a whitelisted user mint far more YUSD than collateral is worth.
hypotheses.impact: Full loss of oracle protection → mint unlimited YUSD for minimal collateral, or redeem for arbitrary collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if `_feedRegistry` is address(0) or if `chainlinkPrice == 0`; do not fall back to user-supplied amounts as a safety path.

hypotheses.title: Blacklisted user blocks redeem approval and traps locked YUSD
hypotheses.description: `approveRedeemRequest` calls `yusd.safeTransfer(insuranceFundAddress, fee)` and `yusd.burn(burnAmount)` on the locked YUSD held by the contract, and `_rejectRedeemRequest`/`withdrawRedeemRequest` call `yusd.safeTransfer(request.order.userWallet, ...)`. If the user is blacklisted in YUSD after creating the request, `_update` reverts on `to` (the user) for reject/withdraw, and the FUNDS_MANAGER cannot approve either because the burn/transfer path also touches the user's locked funds indirectly via accounting. The request becomes stuck in PENDING with `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` permanently inflated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (whitelisted) creates a redeem request. 2) Attacker gets themselves blacklisted (or is blacklisted by owner for unrelated reasons — but the attacker can also cause this by being the blacklisted party). 3) Any call to `approveRedeemRequest`, `rejectRedeemRequest`, or `withdrawRedeemRequest` for that request reverts because `yusd.safeTransfer` to the blacklisted user reverts in `_update`. 4) The request is permanently PENDING; `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` never decreases.
hypotheses.impact: Locked YUSD is permanently stuck in the contract, `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` accounting is corrupted, and the redeem queue for that requestId is frozen. If many users are blacklisted, the contract's YUSD balance becomes unreconcilable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a fallback path (e.g., allow FUNDS_MANAGER to redirect rejected/withdrawn funds to an alternate address, or burn the locked YUSD and credit the user off-chain) so blacklisting cannot permanently freeze the request.

hypotheses.title: Redeem request can be withdrawn after approval, double-spending locked YUSD
hypotheses.description: `withdrawRedeemRequest` only checks `request.status != RedeemRequestStatus.PENDING`, so a request that has already been APPROVED (collateral paid out, YUSD burned) cannot be withdrawn — but the check is on status, and the request struct is stored in storage. The real flaw is that `approveRedeemRequest` sets status to APPROVED and decrements `totalRedeemLockedYUSD`, but the YUSD was already transferred into the contract at request time; the burn uses `burnAmount` (post-fee) while `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` was decremented by the full `order.yusdAmount`. If `redeemFeeBP > 0`, the fee portion of locked YUSD remains in the contract and is never burned nor returned, and `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` accounting diverges from actual locked balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User submits `requestRedeem` with `yusdAmount = X`, locking X YUSD and incrementing `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` by X. 2) FUNDS_MANAGER approves; `burnAmount = X - fee`, fee is transferred to insuranceFund, `totalRedeemLockedYUSD -= X`. 3) The fee YUSD stays in the contract but is no longer tracked as locked. 4) Any subsequent redeem approval can draw on `_untrackedAvailableAssetBalance`/YUSD balance that includes this orphaned fee, effectively letting the protocol pay out collateral against YUSD that was never burned.
hypotheses.impact: YUSD supply is not fully reduced on redeem; the contract accumulates untracked YUSD that can be used to back additional collateral payouts, leading to over-redemption and eventual insolvency of the collateral pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn the full `order.yusdAmount` (or transfer the fee out and burn the remainder) so that `totalRedeemLockedYUSD` always equals the YUSD actually held for pending redeems.

hypotheses.title: _stringToBytes32 truncates IDs causing reward collisions
hypotheses.description: `_stringToBytes32` uses assembly `result := mload(add(source, 32))` which reads the first 32 bytes of the string data. Strings longer than 32 bytes are silently truncated to their first 32 bytes, so two different request IDs that share the same first 32 bytes map to the same `bytes32` id. An attacker who can influence `additionalData` (via a signed order from the trusted signer, or by choosing a requestId in `depositIncome`/`requestRedeem`) can craft two distinct strings with identical first 32 bytes, causing reward amounts to be merged or overwritten. In `depositRewards`, `_rewards[id].amount += amount` merges them; in `claimRewards`, the merged amount is claimable once, so one depositor's rewards are stolen by the other.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets a signed order with additionalData = "A"*32 + "X". 2) Attacker gets another signed order with additionalData = "A"*32 + "Y". 3) Both map to the same bytes32 id. 4) The second deposit adds to the first's reward, and the attacker (or the other user) can claim the combined amount, taking funds not meant for them.
hypotheses.impact: Reward funds can be stolen or misallocated between users due to ID collision; loss of funds for one depositor.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `keccak256(bytes(source))` instead of truncating to 32 bytes, or revert if `bytes(source).length > 32`.

hypotheses.title: claimRewards allows partial claim leaving reward amount inconsistent
hypotheses.description: claimRewards marks _addressClaimedRewards[sender][id] = true on the first claim, then subtracts claimRequest.amounts[i] from _rewards[id].amount. If the user claims less than the full reward, the remaining amount is stranded because the claimed flag prevents any further claim, and the residual can only be swept by withdrawExpiredRewards after expiry. The signature verification does not bind amounts to the reward, so a user can claim an arbitrary amount up to the reward balance, and the leftover is effectively locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker obtains a valid signed ClaimRequest (or reuses one) with amounts[i] smaller than the reward. They claim the small amount, setting the claimed flag. The remaining reward amount is now unclaimable by them and only recoverable by REWARDS_MANAGER after expiry, effectively locking funds.
hypotheses.impact: Reward funds stranded/locked; users lose the unclaimed portion of their rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only set _addressClaimedRewards to true when the full reward amount is claimed, or track claimed amounts per user per id.

hypotheses.title: Missing staleness check on ChainlinkFeedRegistry in YUSD conversion
hypotheses.description: `_getAssetYUSDPriceOracle` calls `_getAssetUSDPriceChainlink(asset)` which uses `chainlinkAssetHeartbeat[asset]`. If `chainlinkAssetHeartbeat` is 0 (default for assets added without heartbeat, or reset on `removeSupportedAsset` then re-added incorrectly), `updatedAt >= block.timestamp - 0` reverts on any positive check but when `address(_feedRegistry)==0` returns `(0,0)`; then `assetUSDPrice*yusdDecimals/yusdPrice` divides a zero, returning 0, and the oracle-price branch is skipped. More critically, when heartbeat is set correctly, the check exists but the function returns the oracle price even if the Chainlink price is from a stale-but-within-heartbeat update combined with a fresh oracle, masking the fact that the underlying reference price is outdated relative to the YUSD oracle which has no staleness check.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker waits for a window where the oracle price (`yusdUSDPrice`) has not been updated to reflect market movement while Chainlink heartbeat still passes; the mispriced min collateral allows unfair redemptions/mints at a favorable ratio.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting / unfair exchange ratio drains collateral or YUSD value.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit staleness validation to the AegisOracle path and ensure both oracles are fresh before computing the combined price.

hypotheses.title: approveRedeemRequest transfers collateral before burning YUSD
hypotheses.description: The function updates request.status and totalRedeemLockedYUSD, then transfers collateral to the user, and only afterwards calls yusd.burn(burnAmount). If the collateral asset has transfer hooks (ERC777/ERC1363), the user's callback executes while the YUSD has not yet been burned, allowing the user to observe/act on still-existing YUSD balance and the already-decremented totalRedeemLockedYUSD. The nonReentrant guard blocks reentry into this contract, but cross-contract reentrancy into AegisRewards or YUSD is possible.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker submits a redeem request with a hook-enabled collateral asset. On approval, the safeTransfer to the attacker triggers a hook that calls into AegisRewards.claimRewards or YUSD.transfer to move the not-yet-burned YUSD, or reads totalRedeemLockedYUSD to manipulate dependent logic.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double-spend of YUSD before burn; accounting mismatch between totalRedeemLockedYUSD and actual locked YUSD.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn YUSD before transferring collateral, or move the burn to immediately after the status update and before the external transfer.

hypotheses.title: Redeem limit period can be reset by anyone via zero-amount boundary
hypotheses.description: `_checkMintRedeemLimit` resets `currentPeriodStartTime` and `currentPeriodTotalAmount` whenever `currentPeriodEndTime <= block.timestamp`. Because `requestRedeem` is callable by any whitelisted user, an attacker can call it with a tiny `yusdAmount` right after a period ends to reset the period, then immediately fill the new period's `maxPeriodAmount` with their own requests, blocking legitimate users for the rest of the period. The same applies to `mint`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for `currentPeriodEndTime` to pass. 2) Attacker calls `requestRedeem` with a minimal amount, triggering the reset branch and starting a fresh period. 3) Attacker (or colluding accounts) immediately consumes the entire `maxPeriodAmount` for the new period. 4) Legitimate users' `requestRedeem` calls revert with `LimitReached` until the next period.
hypotheses.impact: Redeem (and mint) capacity is monopolized by an attacker each period, effectively denying service to honest users and potentially trapping their YUSD if they cannot redeem.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a rolling window or per-user rate limit instead of a single global period counter, or require the period reset to be triggered by a trusted role.
